Threat.value: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, hypervigilance to sudden movements by other people is a poor thematic fit. It suggests an interpersonal/assault-type threat rather than danger linked to environmental cues or disaster reminders.

issues.item: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: Avoiding unfamiliar places because danger cannot be assessed is more consistent with persistent fear of human threat or assault in public settings than with a natural-disaster index trauma. In this profile there are no corresponding disaster-specific trigger or memory items that would make this threat pattern cohere.

issues.item: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
issues.explanation: Self-blame based on one's character is a weak fit for a natural-disaster trauma. Some survivor guilt or responsibility appraisals can occur, but this item implies dispositional blame for an uncontrollable event, which is clinically harder to reconcile here, especially without complementary appraisal content about responsibility or preventability.

issues.item: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items are hard to reconcile as a coherent pair for the same trauma memory. 'Photographic Recall' implies a vivid, detailed, visually accessible memory that feels directly available, whereas 'Memory Feels Alien' suggests marked detachment/disownership of the memory. These can both occur in PTSD, but endorsed together as defining memory qualities for the same event is clinically tense and would likely prompt questioning of coherence. The rest of the profile is broadly consistent with severe post-disaster PTSD, and the Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat/Memory pattern is plausible.

issues.item: Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
issues.explanation: The threat profile is partly coherent for severe PTSD after a natural disaster (hypervigilance to sounds, sleep disturbance), but 'avoiding unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger' fits a generalized danger/assault-style threat schema more than a natural-disaster trauma pattern. For this trauma type, threat is more plausibly cued by weather, environmental instability, or disaster reminders. This item is not impossible, but it is the least coherent with the specified trauma context and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Uncontrolled Access' and 'Fragmented Pieces' suggest intrusive, poorly elaborated trauma memory, which aligns with the formulation. By contrast, 'Memory Feels Alien' implies marked depersonalization/dissociative detachment from the memory. That can occur clinically, but paired with the very high PCL-5 and the rest of the profile it introduces a qualitatively different dissociative presentation that is not supported elsewhere in Threat or Negative Appraisals, making this memory item the least internally coherent in the set.

issues.item: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
issues.explanation: This memory item implies a strong trigger-linked reactivation process, but the formulation explicitly marks Triggers → Memory as inactive. The rest of the profile contains no Triggers items, and the formulation centers the case on Negative Appraisals ↔ Threat/Memory links rather than environmental cue-driven retrieval. For this patient, that item conflicts with the specified formulation structure more than the other selected items do.

vignette:
Maliha is a 52-year-old Southeast Asian American woman who has worked the evening shift at a fast food restaurant for years, steady and reliable in a routine she once found comforting. She is married, and before the disaster she had taken pride in being the calm one in her family, the person who kept going when others were upset. That changed after the hurricane that tore through her neighborhood the previous year. She remembers the night in pieces rather than as a whole: the pressure in the air before landfall, the sudden cracking sound as part of the roof gave way, water pushing under the door, her husband shouting from another room, and the darkness after the power failed. What remains most vivid is not a full story but jagged fragments that intrude without warning—the sound of pounding wind, the slam of debris against the house, the sensation that there was nowhere safe to stand. When those fragments come back, she feels flooded so quickly that she has to stop what she is doing and brace herself until the feeling passes.

In the weeks after the storm, Maliha had come to believe that what happened said something permanent about her life rather than about one terrible night. She was certain that bad things could come at any time and that she had no real way to stop them. She also felt estranged from the world around her, as if other people had resumed ordinary life while she had been left outside it. Even at home with her husband, she often felt detached, telling herself that she would never again feel normal warmth or ease. Those beliefs seemed to open the door to the memory rather than settle it. Whenever she caught herself thinking that nowhere was truly safe and that she could not protect herself, the storm would force its way back in disconnected flashes, as if her mind were proving the point to her.

Her nights became the hardest part of the day. Darkness now feels dangerous to her in a way daylight does not. She lies down tired but cannot settle, listening for changes in the house and tensing at every unexpected sound from outside. A slammed car door, a neighbor’s trash bin tipping, a sudden gust against the siding can jolt her upright before she has time to think. Underneath that vigilance is a conviction that she is still vulnerable, that if something starts again she will be helpless to stop it. Because she has come to see herself as someone to whom catastrophe can simply happen, she scans constantly for signs of danger, especially after sunset, and sleep has become broken and thin.

The memories and the threat feeling now feed each other so tightly that she rarely experiences one without the other close behind. At work, when the ice machine drops a load loudly or someone bangs a metal tray in the kitchen, her body reacts before she can remind herself where she is. She goes rigid, heart racing, and in that instant the storm comes back in shards—the roof cracking, objects hitting the house, her husband yelling in the dark. The more the memory bursts in this way, the more certain she becomes that she has to stay on guard for the next sudden sound. By the end of her shift she is exhausted from listening and watching, yet when she gets home she still cannot let go of the sense that nighttime is when danger finds people.

That same vigilance seems to keep the memories close to the surface. She listens so intently for unexpected noise that every sound becomes a possible beginning, and once her body is keyed up the images break through more easily. Sometimes while closing the restaurant she hears the back door rattle in the wind and instantly loses her place, overcome by emotion so sharply that she has to step into the storage area and wait for herself to come back. She cannot tell the story of the hurricane smoothly even in therapy; it arrives as broken scenes that are too intense to hold onto for long. This, too, has hardened her view that something in her has been permanently altered. She thinks other people can move on because they still belong in ordinary life, while she remains stuck watching for the next blow.

By the time she sought help, the strain was showing both at home and at work. Her husband had begun sleeping through her repeated checking of windows and doors, but he worried about how little she rested and how quickly loud sounds could undo her. At work she has started dreading the evening shift, not because of the tasks themselves but because the restaurant’s clatter and the dark parking lot outside keep her feeling poised for disaster. What finally brought her in was the fear that this was now her permanent future: sleepless, easily shattered by noise, cut off from ordinary feeling, and unable to stop the storm from returning to her mind. What she hopes for, though she says it cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to feel that night become past tense instead of something that is still waiting for her after dark.
